title: The data that writes itself
hook: Two identical districts. One record apart. Where does the model send patrols?

knows: that models learn from past data
doesNotKnow: that a deployed model's decisions can change the data that later retrains it

misconception: If a model's data are real records, its predictions are neutral evidence about reality.
objective: The learner can explain that when a model decides where we look, the records it later learns from reflect its own choices, so a small head start can grow into an apparent fact even when the underlying rates are identical.

claims.text: The toy's rule: two districts with the same true incident rate; records start at A = 6 and B = 5. Each round one patrol goes to the district with more records, and only the patrolled district logs one new incident. This is a simplification invented for the lesson (one log per round, incidents logged only where patrolled).
claims.source: The lesson's own model in Demo.tsx (run(), rule "most").

claims.text: Under that rule A is always ahead, so it gets every patrol: after 20 rounds A has 26 of 31 records (83.9%) and B still has 5.
claims.source: 6 + 20 = 26 versus 5; 26 / 31 = 0.839. Reproduced by running run("most", 20) from Demo.tsx: a 26, b 5, all 20 patrols to A.

claims.text: If patrols take turns (A first), after 20 rounds A has 16 of 31 records (51.6%).
claims.source: A gets 10 patrols and B 10: 16 versus 15, 16 / 31 = 0.516. Reproduced by running run("turns", 20) from Demo.tsx.

claims.text: About real systems: analyses of predictive policing describe the same runaway feedback loop, where patrols sent by past records generate the records that justify more patrols.
claims.source: Lum & Isaac 2016, “To predict and serve?”, Significance 13(5), 14–19; Ensign, Friedler, Neville, Scheidegger & Venkatasubramanian 2018, “Runaway Feedback Loops in Predictive Policing”, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 81 (FAT* 2018).

recall.question: A shop's app shows popular items first, and “popular” is measured by clicks in the app. Why might a new item never become popular?
options: It is rarely shown, so it rarely gets the clicks that would get it shown
recall.why: The model's own choices decide what data it collects. Items it does not show cannot earn the clicks that would change its mind.
